title: Confit de Canard
subtitle: Duck legs slow-cooked in their own fat until fall-apart tender
excerpt: Duck legs salted overnight and then cooked very slowly submerged in duck fat until the meat is completely tender and the skin becomes crisp on reheating. The confit keeps for weeks under its fat layer.
sourceNotes: Confit de canard is a preservation technique from Gascony, in south-west France. Paula Wolfert, The Cooking of South-West France (1983), gives the classic domestic method. Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), documents the technique in the confits section. The method predates refrigeration as a preservation technique; the duck legs could be stored in their fat for several months.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The cured, cooked legs keep in their fat for up to 2 weeks in the fridge. Cover the fat surface completely. Reheat individual legs in a hot frying pan, skin-side down, until the skin crisps and the meat is hot through.

glossaryTerms.definition: A French preservation method in which food (typically duck, goose, or pork) is first cured in salt, then cooked very slowly submerged in its own fat. The fat acts as a seal against air when the food is stored.

projectSchedule.title: Salt the duck legs
projectSchedule.body: Rub the duck legs with salt, thyme, garlic, and bay. Cover and refrigerate overnight.

projectSchedule.title: Slow-cook the duck
projectSchedule.body: Rinse the legs, pat dry, and submerge in duck fat in an oven dish. Cook at 120°C for 2 hours. Leave to cool in the fat.

content.text: Confit de canard is duck legs preserved in duck fat. The process takes two days: the legs cure overnight in salt and aromatics, then cook very slowly submerged in fat until the meat is completely tender. The result is a duck leg that keeps for weeks in the fridge under its fat layer, ready to be crisped in a hot pan whenever you want it. The skin, when reheated correctly, becomes extraordinarily crisp.
is traditionally made with duck fat rendered from other parts of the bird. Jars of duck fat are widely available and make the process straightforward. You need enough fat to fully submerge the legs.

items.prepNote: or enough to submerge the legs

content.text: You will need a deep oven dish or Dutch oven that fits the legs snugly. A close fit means you need less fat to submerge them.

Rub the duck legs all over with 2 tsp of coarse salt per leg. Press the thyme, bay, garlic, and peppercorns against the flesh. Place in a dish, cover, and refrigerate for 8 to 12 hours. Overnight is fine.
Heat the oven to 120°C fan. Rinse the salt cure from the duck legs and pat thoroughly dry. Arrange in a snug oven dish or Dutch oven, skin-side down.
Melt the duck fat and pour it over the legs until they are fully submerged. They should be completely covered. Add more fat if needed.
Cook uncovered in the oven at 120°C for 2 hours until the meat is completely tender and pulls from the bone easily. The fat should barely bubble throughout.
Leave the legs to cool in the fat. Once cool, transfer to a container, cover completely with the strained fat, and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Lift the legs from the fat and let any excess fat drain off. Place skin-side down in a cold cast-iron skillet. Set over medium heat. As the fat renders, the heat gradually rises and the skin crisps without burning. Cook for 10 to 12 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and crackling. Turn and warm the flesh side for 3 to 4 minutes. Serve with lentils, roasted potatoes, or a green salad.

items.symptom: The skin does not crisp when reheating
items.cause: The pan was not hot enough, or fat from the confit prevented the skin from drying out.
items.fix: Start in a cold dry pan and heat slowly. The fat renders from the skin as the temperature rises, so the skin fries in its own fat. If starting in a hot pan, the skin can seal before the fat has a chance to render.

items.symptom: The meat is tough after 2 hours in the oven
items.cause: The oven temperature was too high, causing the fat to boil rather than barely simmer.
items.fix: Reduce the temperature to 110°C and cook for a further 30 to 45 minutes. The fat should move only slightly at the surface. A rapid simmer toughens the meat.

items.cause: The cure was left on too long, or the legs were not rinsed thoroughly before cooking.
items.fix: Rinse the cured legs thoroughly in cold water and pat dry before cooking. 8 to 12 hours of curing is enough; longer than 18 hours can over-salt the meat.

items.symptom: The fat turned cloudy when storing
items.cause: There was some moisture in the fat or the container.
items.fix: Cloudy fat is not spoiled; moisture has simply mixed in. Remelt the fat gently, strain through a sieve, and return to the container. The legs keep best when fully submerged in fat that is clear and dry.

content.text: Confit de canard is the signature dish of Gascony, the south-west corner of France running from Bordeaux toward the Pyrenees. The region raises more Gascony ducks than anywhere else, and the tradition of preserving them in their own fat is ancient, long predating refrigeration. The confit is one of the three Gascon gifts to French cooking, alongside foie gras and Armagnac. Today it is sold ready-prepared in tins and jars across France, but the home-made version has a different quality: the cure is lighter and the flesh more supple.
